AWS BILL CHANGE EXPLAINER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Why did my AWS bill go up?

Download the cost-by-service CSV from AWS Cost Explorer for two months, paste it here, and see the lines that explain the change, ranked, with what is new, what is gone, and a checklist of what usually moves each service.

Nothing is uploaded. The file you load is read in this browser and never leaves your device. It ranks the numbers you give it — it cannot see why a line moved.

1. Load your Cost Explorer export

In Cost Explorer: group by Service, granularity Monthly, pick at least two months, then Download CSV.

Have one file per month instead?

Fill both days fields when the later month is not finished. The page then compares per-day rates, scaling the earlier period to the length of the later one.

2. What moved

Check your file

Every line, biggest move first

LineStatusBeforeAfterChange%Share of rise

Where to look first

Run it on a schedule

Same engine, zero dependencies, one file. Fails the job when the bill rises past a number you choose, so a monthly script can tell you before the invoice does:

node cli.mjs compare export.csv                          # last two periods
node cli.mjs compare july.csv august.csv                 # one period per file
node cli.mjs compare export.csv --after-days 12 --before-days 31   # half-finished month
node cli.mjs compare export.csv --max-increase-pct 15 --max-increase-usd 500

Get cli.mjs and engine.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call, ever. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 over a threshold, 2 unreadable file or bad option.

Common questions

Why did my AWS bill go up?

Export the cost by service for the two months from Cost Explorer (Download CSV), paste it here, and the page ranks every line by how much it moved, so the two or three lines that explain most of the rise are at the top. It then lists the common causes for each of those services as a checklist. It cannot see why a line moved; it tells you where to look.

Which file does it need?

The CSV from AWS Cost Explorer's Download CSV button, grouped by Service (or linked account, region or usage type), with monthly granularity and at least two months. You can also paste two separate exports, one period each.

What if the current month is only half over?

Then comparing it with a full month makes the bill look like it fell. Enter the number of days in each period and the page compares per-day rates instead, scaling the earlier period to the length of the later one.

Is my bill uploaded anywhere?

No. The page reads what you paste or load in your browser and makes no network request. The CLI reads a local file and makes no network call.

Why is Tax, Support or a Savings Plan line flagged differently?

Those lines move because of other lines or a contract, not because something new started running. Support is usually a percentage of the rest of your usage, and a credit or commitment that ended makes the bill rise with no change in usage. The page says so instead of sending you hunting for a service.

Can it fail a CI job or a scheduled report?

Yes. The CLI takes --max-increase-usd and --max-increase-pct and exits 1 when the net rise is above either, so a monthly script can alert you when the bill jumps.

Compared with the AWS console or a paid FinOps tool? See the comparison page. Planning a change instead of explaining one? Price a Terraform plan with the Terraform Plan Cost Estimate.

vs-cost-explorer.html.text:
← AWS Bill Change Explainer

This tool vs. the Cost Explorer console

Different jobs. The AWS console is where spend lives and where you explore it. This is a small, offline tool for one question: which lines explain the change between two periods in an export you already downloaded.

What each one is for

The Cost Explorer console is AWS's own interface for exploring spend. You can group and filter by service, account, region, tag and usage type, chart it, and download the result as CSV. It has the live data.

This tool reads that CSV, in a browser page or a single Node.js file, ranks every line by how much it moved between two periods, scales an unfinished month so it is not mistaken for a drop, names what is new and what is gone, and lists common causes for the services that rose. It has no data of its own.

QuestionThis toolCost Explorer console
Where the data comes fromA CSV you export and pasteYour live billing data
Ranking the movers between two periodsYes, one table, biggest move first, with share of the risePossible by comparing charts and filters yourself
Half-finished monthCompares per-day rates when you give the day countsYou adjust for it yourself
What usually moves this serviceA checklist per common service (not a diagnosis)No; you bring the knowledge
Drill into tags, accounts, usage typesOnly the dimension in your exportYes
Live data, budgets, forecastsNoYes
Fail a script when the bill jumpsYes: --max-increase-usd and --max-increase-pct exit 1Alerts and budgets are available in AWS; check its docs for current options
NetworkNone. The export never leaves your deviceRuns in your AWS account

Use this when you have a CSV and one question, or want a monthly script to flag a jump. Use the console when you need live data, tags, drill-down or budgets. Use both: find the line here, then drill into it there.

Statements about the AWS console summarise its public documentation as best understood when this page was written and may be out of date. Check AWS's documentation for the current feature set.

Common questions

Is this a replacement for Cost Explorer?

No. Cost Explorer is where the data comes from, and its own console can group, filter and chart spend interactively. This tool takes the CSV it exports and does one narrow job: rank two periods against each other, normalise a partial month, and list what usually moves each service.

When is this tool the better fit?

When you want the answer to one question, which lines explain the rise, without clicking through filters, or when you want a script to flag a jump every month. It also helps when the bill must not leave your machine.

Does it replace a FinOps platform?

No. Paid FinOps and cost-management products describe features such as anomaly detection on live data, allocation by tag or team, budgets, and savings recommendations. This tool has none of that: it compares two periods in a file.

Can I use both?

Yes. Use Cost Explorer or a platform to see live data and set budgets, and use this to explain a specific month-over-month jump from an export.

Open the AWS Bill Change Explainer with your own export, or price a change before you make it with the Terraform Plan Cost Estimate.
